vjimc-1994-cat2-01.title: Vieta jumping from $(1,1,1)$
vjimc-1994-cat2-01.body:
**The jump.** Fix $x,y$. The equation is the quadratic $z^2-3xy\,z+(x^2+y^2)=0$ in $z$. If $z$ is one integer root, then by Vieta's formulas the other root is $z'=3xy-z$, also an integer. So if $(x,y,z)$ is a solution, so is $(x,y,3xy-z)$, and by symmetry the same holds for each of the three variables.

**Building up.** Start with the obvious solution $(1,1,1)$. At each step keep the entry $1$ and the largest entry $b$, and replace the remaining entry $c$ by $3\cdot1\cdot b-c$:
$$(1,1,1)\to(1,1,2)\to(1,2,5)\to(1,5,13)\to(1,13,34)\to(1,34,89)\to(1,89,233)$$
(e.g. $3\cdot2-1=5$, $3\cdot5-2=13$, $3\cdot 89-34=233$). Finally replace the $1$ in $(1,89,233)$:
$$1\mapsto 3\cdot89\cdot233-1=62210 .$$
So $(x,y,z)=(89,233,62210)$ is a solution with all entries greater than $50$.

**Check.** $89^2+233^2=7921+54289=62210$, so
$$x^2+y^2+z^2=62210+62210^2=62210\cdot62211,$$
and $3xyz=3\cdot89\cdot233\cdot62210=62211\cdot62210$. ✓

**Answer:** e.g. $(89,233,62210)$ (any permutation; other examples are $(233,610,426389)$ and $(169,985,499393)$). A computer search shows that no solution has all three entries in $(50,300)$, so some entry must be large.

vjimc-1994-cat2-02.title: A linear recurrence
vjimc-1994-cat2-02.body:
Let $\lambda_{1,2}=\frac{3\pm\sqrt{17}}2$. They are the roots of $t^2-3t-2=0$ (sum $3$, product $\frac{9-17}{4}=-2$), so $\lambda_i^{n+2}=3\lambda_i^{n+1}+2\lambda_i^n$. Adding these for $i=1,2$, the numbers $a_n=\lambda_1^n+\lambda_2^n$ satisfy
$$a_{n+2}=3a_{n+1}+2a_n,\qquad a_0=2,\quad a_1=\lambda_1+\lambda_2=3 .$$
By induction all $a_n$ are integers. Modulo $2$ the recurrence reads $a_{n+2}\equiv a_{n+1}\pmod 2$, so for $n\ge1$,
$$a_n\equiv a_{n-1}\equiv\dots\equiv a_1=3\equiv1\pmod 2 .$$
Thus $a_n$ is an odd integer for every $n\in\mathbb N=\{1,2,\dots\}$. (For $n=0$ one gets $a_0=2$, so $n\ge1$ is needed.) First values: $3,13,45,161,\dots$ ∎

vjimc-1994-cat2-02.title: Binomial expansion of $(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)^n$
vjimc-1994-cat2-02.body:
With $a_m$ integers as above (from the recurrence) and $\lambda_1\lambda_2=-2$, expand
$$3^n=(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)^n=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk\lambda_1^k\lambda_2^{n-k}=a_n+\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\binom nk\lambda_1^k\lambda_2^{n-k}.$$
Pair the terms $k$ and $n-k$ for $1\le k<\frac n2$:
$$\binom nk\left(\lambda_1^k\lambda_2^{n-k}+\lambda_1^{n-k}\lambda_2^k\right)=\binom nk(\lambda_1\lambda_2)^k a_{n-2k}=\binom nk(-2)^k a_{n-2k},$$
and if $n$ is even the middle term is $\binom n{n/2}(-2)^{n/2}$. All these are even integers (each contains a factor $(-2)^k$, $k\ge1$). Hence $a_n=3^n-(\text{even integer})$ is odd. ∎

vjimc-1994-cat2-03.title: Substitute $y=0$ and $y=1$
vjimc-1994-cat2-03.body:
**$y=0$** (allowed for $x\ne0$): $f(0)=\frac{f(x)+f(0)}{x}$, i.e.
$$f(x)=(x-1)f(0)\qquad(x\ne0).\tag{1}$$
In particular $f(1)=0$.

**$y=1$** (allowed for $x\ne-1$): $f(x)=\frac{f(x)+f(1)}{x+1}=\frac{f(x)}{x+1}$, so $(x+1)f(x)=f(x)$, i.e.
$$x\,f(x)=0\qquad(x\ne-1).\tag{2}$$
So $f(x)=0$ for all $x\ne0,-1$.

**The remaining points.** By (1) with $x=2$: $0=f(2)=f(0)$, so $f(0)=0$. Then (1) with $x=-1$ gives $f(-1)=-2f(0)=0$.

Hence $f\equiv0$, which indeed satisfies the equation (both sides are $0$).

**Answer: No**, $f(x)=0$ for every $x$. ∎

vjimc-1994-cat2-04.title: Study the derivative
vjimc-1994-cat2-04.body:
Let $f(x)=1+x+\frac{x^2}2+\dots+\frac{x^n}n$. Then
$$f'(x)=1+x+x^2+\dots+x^{n-1}=\frac{x^n-1}{x-1}\quad(x\ne1),\qquad f'(1)=n .$$

**$n$ odd.** Then $x^n-1$ and $x-1$ have the same sign for every $x\ne1$ (as $x\mapsto x^n$ is increasing), so $f'(x)>0$ for all $x$. Hence $f$ is strictly increasing; since $f$ has odd degree with positive leading coefficient, $f(x)\to-\infty$ as $x\to-\infty$ and $f(x)\to+\infty$ as $x\to+\infty$. By the intermediate value theorem $f$ has exactly **one** real root.

**$n$ even.** Now $x^n-1>0$ for $|x|>1$ and $<0$ for $|x|<1$. Hence $f'(x)<0$ for $x<-1$, $f'(x)>0$ for $-1<x<1$ and $x>1$ (and $f'(1)=n>0$), $f'(-1)=0$. So $f$ decreases on $(-\infty,-1]$ and increases on $[-1,\infty)$: its global minimum is
$$f(-1)=1-1+\frac12-\frac13+\frac14-\dots-\frac1{n-1}+\frac1n=\left(\frac12-\frac13\right)+\left(\frac14-\frac15\right)+\dots+\left(\frac1{n-2}-\frac1{n-1}\right)+\frac1n>0,$$
every bracket being positive. So $f>0$ everywhere and $f$ has **no** real roots.

**Answer:** one real root for odd $n$, no real root for even $n$. (A computer check of $n=1,\dots,11$ confirms $1,0,1,0,\dots$.) ∎
